entry.title: AI: A Guide to Constructing a Universe — A Journey from 0 to 9

link.title: AI: A Guide to Constructing a Universe — A Journey from 0 to 9

entry.content:
Contents

  • What can a flower teach you about building a universe?
  • Outside, within, and outward again
  • Numbers can tell you more than “how many”
  • A universe in ten movements
  • Responsibilities, records, and tools
  • Try it with a learning companion
  • The macro reflected in the micro
  • What universe will you construct?
  • References and further reading

What can a flower teach you about building a universe?

Put a flower, a drawing, and a piece of software side by side. What could they have in common?

Start with something you can see: parts arranged into a whole. Petals have an arrangement. A drawing gives relationships a shape. Software brings separate contributions into something people can use.

Michael S. Schneider’s A Beginner’s Guide to Constructing the Universe invites a journey through number and geometry in nature, art, and science. We’ll borrow that spirit of exploration to ask: how do we turn a world we encounter into a world we understand—and then into something we create?

The cover’s human and digital hands surround a world of ideas and creations. Imagine the numbers around it as invitations to look again: at unity, relationships, structure, change, and renewal.

Our journey uses 0–9 as ten responsibilities for inquiry. These are our design choices, not ten built-in AI modules or a claim that AI experiences the world as we do.

Follow the story first. Open the deck and diagrams when you want a closer look.

Outside, within, and outward again

Imagine finding a seed. You watch it grow, sketch what you notice, and use that sketch to plan a garden. The garden gives you something new to observe.

You’ve moved through three connected worlds: what you encounter outside, what it means to you within, and what you give form to outwardly. A drawing, story, calendar, or tool can carry an understanding beyond the moment that produced it.

Encounter → interpretation → expression → renewed encounter. The movement returns: what you make changes what you meet, and what you already believe shapes what you notice.

See how encounter, interpretation, and expression connect

An editorial relationship model, not a mechanism of consciousness.

Numbers can tell you more than “how many”

Try a tiny drawing experiment. Make one dot, then another. Join them. Add a third dot away from the line and connect all three.

You haven’t merely counted to three. You’ve moved from a focus, to a relationship, to a form. Close a circle around the drawing and ask which parts belong together. Geometry gives your thinking something you can see and examine.

Number tells you how many; Schneider also invites you to consider what kind of relationship a pattern expresses—wholeness, polarity, structure, balance, or growth. His introduction connects that exploration to nature and human expression. That is the curiosity we want to carry into this article.

📚 Reference · Number as quality

A Beginner’s Guide to Constructing the Universe invites us to read number through geometric patterns in nature, art, and science. Its cover introduces the visual language that inspires this chapter’s inquiry into relationships.

Michael S. Schneider · Cover thumbnail via Google Books.

The book’s journey follows 1–10, connecting numerical qualities with geometric forms and their appearances in nature, art, and science. Its later chapter themes include regeneration, organization, renewal, and a horizon beyond what has already been formed.

We take that invitation into AI design. A shared goal gives work unity. Sources introduce relationships. Interpretation gives those relationships meaning. A plan gives them structure. Action changes the situation, and review asks what that change revealed.

Our map is 0–9, not a renumbered summary of Schneider’s chapters. We add 0 for the openness before a question takes shape. The geometric bridges are memory aids and design metaphors; resemblance alone does not prove a shared meaning across cultures or a law of computation.

Where the inspiration comes from

The Book of Wisdom sparked the symbolic exploration; Krishnamurti’s observation and conditioning invites questioning assumptions; Bohm’s On Dialogue encourages shared meaning. They inspire our interpretation. From Secret of the Sphinx, keep three questions: what needs to change, what did we overlook, and what happens when we act? Human attention, task focus, and neural attention remain distinct.

A universe in ten movements

Now picture constructing a small world of your own: a garden, a story, or a learning tool. Before choosing software components, follow the movement of the idea:

  • 0–3 · Let a possibility become meaningful. Leave room for the unknown, choose a direction, find relationships, and ask what they mean.
  • 4–6 · Give it form and let it change. Plan a structure, act, and bring the resulting pieces together.
  • 7–9 · Examine what you made. Check its support, make a result available, and carry what you learned toward the next question.

These are questions to revisit, not a required execution order. Open the illustrated deck to explore how each quality becomes a human question and an AI responsibility. One participant can serve several responsibilities.

Explore the ten illustrated responsibilities · 0–9
  1. 0

    Openness

    What is unknown or possible?

    Before the first mark on the page, there is room for something you haven’t imagined yet.

    Explore details

    List unknowns, possible starting points, and available capabilities.

    Resources
    Questions · Capability registry · Limits
    Actors
    Explorer

    Limit. An available tool may be unsuitable or wrong. Preserve uncertainty.

  2. 1

    Unity & Direction

    What are we trying to create?

    A circle holds parts together; a shared purpose gives an inquiry its unity.

    Explore details

    Agree on the goal, scope, constraints, and success criteria.

    Resources
    Goals · Instructions · Success criteria
    Actors
    Human + Clarifier

    Limit. Revise the goal if you discover you chose the wrong problem.

  3. 2

    Relation & Context

    What does this depend on?

    Two points invite a connection. Context asks what that connection depends on.

    Explore details

    Gather relevant sources and history. RAG supplies retrieved context; provenance records its origin.

    Resources
    RAG · Search · Sources · Provenance
    Actors
    Researcher

    Limit. Check relevance, freshness, and reliability.

  4. 3

    Meaning

    How do the ideas connect?

    A third point can turn a line into a triangle. Interpretation gives relationships a form you can examine.

    Explore details

    Propose interpretations. Embeddings find similar material; semantic graphs record explicit relationships.

    Resources
    LLM · Embeddings · Semantic graph
    Actors
    Interpreter

    Limit. Similarity does not establish meaning or truth.

  5. 4

    Structure

    What form and plan will support it?

    A boundary makes room for a construction. A plan gives your idea somewhere to stand.

    Explore details

    Define data shapes, expectations, work steps, and allowed transitions.

    Resources
    Schemas · State machines · Workflow plans
    Actors
    Planner

    Limit. A required field can contain a wrong answer. Review the plan.

  6. 5

    Transformation

    What happens when we act?

    An idea changes when it meets the world. Action lets the world answer back.

    Explore details

    Use authorized tools to act and observe; a sandbox bounds the experiment.

    Resources
    Tools · APIs · MCP · Sandbox
    Actors
    Executor

    Limit. A successful call does not prove the problem was solved.

  7. 6

    Organization & Integration

    How do the parts work together?

    Pieces become a working whole through their relationships. Integration keeps those relationships visible.

    Explore details

    Coordinate dependencies and connect contributions into a working account.

    Resources
    Orchestration · Evidence links · Synthesis
    Actors
    Coordinator + Synthesizer

    Limit. Keep disagreements visible. Agent agreement is not independent evidence.

  8. 7

    Discernment

    What is supported, uncertain, or missing?

    Step back from the pattern you prefer. Discernment asks what actually supports it.

    Explore details

    Assess claims against criteria with tests, evaluations, and human review.

    Resources
    Validators · Tests · Evals · Human review
    Actors
    Verifier

    Limit. Checks have limits. More investigation or a pause may be appropriate.

  9. 8

    Realization & Renewal

    What can we deliver and improve?

    Give the idea outward form, then notice what use reveals. Realization opens the possibility of renewal.

    Explore details

    Deliver an inspectable artifact and observe feedback from use.

    Resources
    Artifacts · Authorized actions · Feedback
    Actors
    Producer

    Limit. Live changes need authorization. An artifact is not the intended outcome.

  10. 9

    Synthesis & Horizon

    What have we learned; what remains open?

    A finished page can open another question. The horizon carries understanding beyond this attempt.

    Explore details

    Record findings, limits, and open questions for the next inquiry.

    Resources
    Completion review · Revision · Next inquiry
    Actors
    Reviewer

    Limit. Recorded feedback does not automatically retrain a model.

The illustrations are conceptual aids, not implemented systems or verified results.

Pause and try it: an agent finds a relevant lesson. Which responsibility retrieves it? Which checks whether it supports the proposed exercise?

Responsibilities, records, and tools

You can now see the workshop behind the metaphor. The responsibilities stay available while the creation changes. Sources bring something of the outside world into view; interpretations connect it to a working account; tools give decisions outward form. An inquiry record preserves the goal, observations, decisions, and questions between visits.

Semantics asks what the account means; epistemic responsibility asks what supports it. Humans provide intention and judgment. Tools supply operations, memory supplies continuity, and permissions and budgets bound the work.

Explore the inquiry record, tools, and three perspectives
Part of the record What to keep
Intent Goal, scope, constraints, success criteria
Context Sources, provenance, relevant history
Questions Known gaps and remaining unknowns
Interpretations Candidate meanings and explanations
Evidence Observations linked to claims they support or challenge
Decisions Actions, reasons, permissions, reviews
Results Artifacts, consequences, limits, follow-up questions

The record can span repositories, services, and logs; every model call need not receive its whole history.

Resource Useful role and limit
Memory Keeps history; check for stale or mistaken records
Skills, SDKs, hooks Reuse procedures and connect components; define task fit and scope
Security Bounds actions; tool access does not grant authorization
Observability Exposes behavior; traces do not prove conclusions
Budgets Bounds resources; limits may require a pause

MCP connects external capabilities; tools and APIs perform operations, while RAG supplies retrieved context.

Three distinct architectural roles

Responsibility

A persistent obligation, such as checking support for a conclusion. It remains available when an inquiry returns or branches.

Participant

A human, agent or component contributes within a scope. One agent can serve several responsibilities; a number does not require a separate agent.

Inquiry state

The evolving account of intention, context, questions, interpretations, evidence, decisions and results.

One inquiry, three perspectives

Semantic view

What does the request mean? Preserve relevant entities, concepts and relationships, and keep interpretations revisable as context changes.

Epistemic view

What supports the account? Link observations to claims, retain provenance, and make uncertainties, conflicts and limits inspectable.

Operational view

What may the system do? Coordinate appropriate capabilities, permissions and budgets, then inspect the consequences of actions.

Explore the proposed inquiry architecture

CoALA describes memory, action spaces, and decision-making. Building Effective Agents distinguishes workflows from agents directing tool use. Choose components for the actual task; a classifier may need no agent loop.

Components update the inquiry; memory and traces preserve continuity. A central drawing does not require a central database.

A responsibility asks “What needs attention?” A state asks “Where does the investigation stand?” Missing evidence can reopen investigation; missing access can require a pause.

Explore the inquiry lifecycle

States describe the investigation’s condition; numbers on transitions identify contributing responsibilities, not a mandatory order. Preserve the reason for a pause.

Try it with a learning companion

Let’s give the journey a concrete creation: a learning companion that helps a student practice fractions. A student’s answer is something encountered; an explanation of the difficulty is an interpretation; a new exercise is an outward creation. Its use brings another encounter.

This is a design scenario, not a tested educational system. Start with authorized materials, a few candidate exercises, educator review, and a simple interface.

An orchestrator tracks dependencies, permissions, and pending decisions. It routes work to suitable participants; it isn’t an eleventh responsibility or a requirement for ten separate agents. Software tests check behavior; educator review checks content. Neither alone proves improved learning.

Follow the responsibilities through discovery and delivery
Responsibility Example contribution
**0 · Openness** List unknowns about the student, materials, and possible approaches
**1 · Direction** Agree on the learning objective, scope, boundaries, and success criteria
**2 · Context** Find authorized materials and record sources and permissions
**3 · Meaning** Consider competing explanations of an observed wrong answer
**4 · Structure** Plan a small lesson, component contracts, and review criteria
**5 · Transformation** Build a bounded prototype and candidate exercises with permitted tools
**6 · Integration** Connect sources, versions, contributions, and disagreements
**7 · Discernment** Check factual support, curriculum alignment, accessibility, and behavior
**8 · Realization** Present a reviewed activity after release authorization; gather consented feedback
**9 · Horizon** Record findings, unproven assumptions, and the next question

Before building, check accessible materials and keep explanations of difficulty provisional. Ask the human to review a narrow scope. A planner defines inputs, contracts, and review criteria before concurrent work begins. Link versions to observations and decisions; publication needs authorization and feedback needs appropriate consent.

Explore the multi-agent orchestration

Illustrative exchange, not an execution trace. The orchestrator follows a changing inquiry, not just the next agent call.

Let evidence change the plan

Suppose the software tests pass, but an educator finds that the exercises require advanced reading skills. That suggests a design mismatch, not necessarily weak mathematical understanding. Review at 7 reopens interpretation at 3 and planning at 4; the affected exercises are revised and reviewed again.

A wrong answer is an observation. “The student doesn’t understand fractions” is a claim that needs support.

See how observations support or challenge a claim

Relevant observations bear on a claim; incomplete or conflicting support keeps the question open. Agent agreement alone does not validate it.

Try it: what would help distinguish a mathematical difficulty from a confusingly worded question? Educational effectiveness still needs appropriate evaluation, informed participation, and care with student information.

The macro reflected in the micro

Think of the garden and its seed again: one whole can contain smaller worlds to examine. Building the learning companion can include an inquiry into a single exercise, with its own question, observations, and result. That smaller account should carry evidence back to the larger one.

This is our practical use of the macro–micro analogy: a responsibility pattern can recur at different scopes. Whether every scope needs all ten distinctions remains open.

What universe will you construct?

Choose something you want to understand or make. Start with one observation, draw its relationships, and give a possible interpretation a form you can test. Ask: what changed between the world I encountered and the world I created?

That is the thread connecting this exploration to Schneider’s invitation: number and geometry can help us notice, relate, and express. Our AI map carries the invitation into a workshop of questions, evidence, tools, and human judgment.

Keep sources distinct from claims and artifacts from outcomes. A useful map leaves room for uncertainty and stopping. Its value is what it helps you see—and the better question it lets you ask next.

References and further reading

Symbolism and number

  • Harry B. Joseph / Revival of Wisdom: official platform, the contemporary starting point for our discussion.
  • Michael S. Schneider: A Beginner’s Guide to Constructing the Universe—author’s introduction; book preview and contents.

Observation and shared meaning

  • J. Krishnamurti: The Core of the Teachings, written in 1980.
  • David Bohm: On Dialogue.

AI architecture

  • Sumers et al.: Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents.
  • Anthropic: Building Effective Agents.
  • Model Context Protocol: official introduction.

Related explorations

  • Architecture of the Mind: A Visual Model Through Ruby and Systems Thinking.
  • Secret of the Sphinx.

Source note: the ten responsibilities and symbolic bridges are editorial interpretations. Technical sources support the described architectural functions, rather than the number assignments.
entry.summary: From patterns in nature to ideas and creations: a friendly journey through number, geometry, human inquiry, and ten responsibilities for AI.

entry.title: The AI-Native Engineering Journey: From Understanding to Evidence-Driven Software Evolution

link.title: The AI-Native Engineering Journey: From Understanding to Evidence-Driven Software Evolution

entry.content:
Contents

  • From understanding to accountable engineering
  • 1. Engineering Judgment Beyond Prompts
  • 2. Context, Architecture and Understanding
  • 3. AI Assets and Bounded Agentic Workflows
  • 4. Evidence, Verification and Engineering Risk
  • 5. Evolving Existing Software Through Integrated Workflows
  • 6. AI-Native Products Versus AI-Native Engineering
  • Transfer
  • Conclusion
  • Related reading
  • References

From understanding to accountable engineering

AI-Native Engineering is not merely about building software with AI. It is about transforming software engineering itself into an intent-driven, understanding-centered, and evidence-grounded process. Engineers increasingly coordinate agents, tools, and integrated workflows to investigate, plan, implement, test, and evolve systems while retaining responsibility for judgment, governance, and outcomes.

This changes the interface to engineering work: beyond editing code directly, the engineer can express intent, supply context, authorize bounded actions, inspect evidence, and revise understanding. The code remains essential, and direct programming remains appropriate whenever it is safer, simpler, or more precise. The shift is in how capabilities are orchestrated, not in handing accountability to a model.

The engineering environment can span ChatGPT, GitHub, IDEs, CI/CD, Skills, Hooks, MCP integrations, and SDKs, depending on the actual tools and permissions available. These are examples of potential components—not proof that a single platform supports every capability, nor a mandatory architecture. This standalone article develops the engineering practice without reproducing the symbolic narrative of The Developer’s AI Journey.

🧭 Reader question — role, process, or product?

Before choosing a label, ask what it describes: the developer’s role, the engineering workflow, or the capabilities of the software being built.

Predict before reading: If a team builds an LLM-powered support assistant using conventional pull requests, while another team uses coding agents to maintain an ordinary Rails app, which team is practicing “AI-Native Engineering”? The answer depends on what the phrase describes: the product or the way the product is engineered. We will separate these dimensions before the end.

For now, focus on a less fashionable and more useful question: What do we need to know before we allow an intelligent tool to change a working system?

We will follow a fictional Rails application that processes payment events in Sidekiq. A worker occasionally receives the same logical event twice. The business requirement is not “make the job run once”; it is “prevent duplicate financial effects while preserving legitimate retries and an audit trail.”

This is a deliberate choice. The safest solution to this problem might be deterministic code and a database constraint, not an LLM in production. AI can still help investigate, propose and review the change. The difference between using AI and depending on AI for correctness is the heart of this journey.

1. Engineering Judgment Beyond Prompts

The suggestion looks good. Would you ship it?

Imagine a coding assistant proposing the following change to a payment job:

# Illustrative pseudocode — not production-ready or executed.
def perform(event_id)
  return if PaymentEvent.exists?(external_id: event_id)
  PaymentEvent.create!(external_id: event_id)
  # Apply the payment effect...
end

It looks reasonable. But two workers could check exists? before either creates the record. Depending on the effect’s location and persistence guarantees, both could perform it. The method’s readability says little about its concurrency behavior.

Predict: Does a passing unit test with one invocation establish the “no duplicate effect” requirement? No. The test has not explored simultaneous calls, crash/retry windows, or partial external effects.

The engineering work is to specify the invariant, locate its authoritative enforcement boundary, identify failure paths and design evidence. Generated code is a candidate. Your review must answer whether the candidate protects the real business rule.

This matters beyond payment systems. AI-assisted development can make an initial solution easier to obtain without eliminating review cost. Research on AI and productivity is mixed and context-sensitive. For example, the METR study of experienced open-source developers in early 2025 examined a particular set of tasks, developers and tools; its findings should not be generalized to every developer or present-day model. DORA 2025 examines AI adoption in a broader organizational context, not the same experimental question. Verify exact numerical statements against their original methods before inserting them here.

Try this: Take a generated refactor from a test-backed Rails method. List one assumption about domain behavior, one untested failure path, and one observation that would change your assessment.

Checkpoint: Can you name a claim made by the suggested implementation and the evidence still missing to accept it?

2. Context, Architecture and Understanding

Why did the model miss the invariant?

“Fix duplicate payments” is an instruction. It is not yet sufficient context. An investigation needs to ask what counts as the same logical event, whether duplicate deliveries are expected, how events are persisted, when external calls occur, and what must remain observable when a retry fails.

Sidekiq’s official best-practices guidance explains why jobs should be idempotent: job execution is at least once, not an exactly-once guarantee. That property is easy to say but demanding to implement at the correct business boundary.

Write down the Use Case:

Field Hypothetical payment scenario
Actor / trigger Event delivery or job retry
Goal Apply one legitimate business effect per event
Exception flow Duplicate delivery, concurrent processing, timeout or crash
Constraint Audit the decision without discarding legitimate work
Evidence needed Persistence invariant, concurrency test, trace of side-effect boundaries

The Use Case describes a situation and its outcomes. Intent says what must hold. Inquiry uncovers unknowns. Engineering tests and implements bounded changes. Evidence supports specific claims; understanding may change as new observations arrive. These are complementary roles, not synonyms.

Context map — a model needs more than the job body

Conceptual investigation map, not a diagram of executed tool calls. Files and logs provide candidate evidence; they do not certify a business invariant by themselves.

Try this: Compare the prompts “fix retry duplicates” and “inspect the job, database uniqueness rules, transaction boundary and tests in read-only mode; report unknowns before recommending changes.” What new questions become visible?

Checkpoint: Repository files and logs are useful sources. Which of their contents are actual observations, and which are interpretations not yet verified?

3. AI Assets and Bounded Agentic Workflows

It can run commands. Should we let it?

An assistant that drafts code and an agent that can invoke tools are not the same engineering capability. Permission to read, write, execute, publish or spend resources requires deliberate boundaries.

A useful mental model groups the supporting assets into three complementary lenses:

Understanding Execution Trust
Repository instructions, documented conventions, reusable Skills and domain context Agents, tool workflows, MCP connections and orchestration SDKs Permissions, Hooks where supported, tests, Evals, CI, auditability and observability
What does the assistant need to know? What bounded action may it perform? What has actually been checked, and who decides what happens next?

These are editorial categories, not a formal vendor specification. MCP concerns integration and protocol contracts, not automatic authorization or correctness. GitHub Copilot agent mode documentation describes product capabilities; exact availability and controls depend on versions and settings and must be rechecked for the target host before publication.

For the Rails scenario, start narrow:

Inspect the worker, relevant models, migrations and specs. Do not edit files or run deployment commands. Identify the business idempotency key, possible duplicate side effects and unverified assumptions. Return a proposed change and tests for human review.

Once the inquiry is reviewed, a separate, explicitly authorized step may produce a diff. A test runner’s exit code is one observation, not evidence that every relevant case was covered.

🧰 Try this — permission boundary

Read: inspect jobs, migrations, specs and logs. Propose: report hypotheses and a reviewable plan. Write: only after approval. Release: a distinct human-authorized decision. The boundaries are examples to adapt to your actual environment.

Try this: Design one read-only task, one write-capable task and a separate human release gate. Which tool calls would be refused in each state?

Checkpoint: A tool call completed successfully. Which additional checks would establish whether the action was appropriate and the output reliable?

4. Evidence, Verification and Engineering Risk

The tests passed. What exactly do we know?

Rails transactions can make a group of database operations atomic within the transaction’s scope. They cannot reverse an already delivered HTTP request or other external effect simply because the database rolls back. See the Active Record transaction documentation.

Consider a proposed remedy: define a stable business idempotency key and enforce its uniqueness at the authoritative persistence boundary. Review how an external payment call, a database commit and the Sidekiq acknowledgment interact. An outbox-style design might help a particular integration, but it should be presented as a candidate architecture, not a solution established by this article.

🔎 Claim ≠ Evidence ≠ Understanding

Claim: “Retries cannot duplicate the business effect.”
Evidence required: database guarantees plus executed failure-seeking tests in the relevant environment.
Unknown: external service semantics, crash windows, concurrency assumptions.
Understanding: the provisional interpretation that can be revised when observations disagree.

A useful evidence ledger distinguishes:

Claim Possible evidence Still unknown
Two simultaneous jobs cannot create duplicate ledger entries A verified database constraint and a successfully executed concurrent test Real transaction isolation, production schema and external effects
Failed work can be retried safely Executed retry and recovery scenarios Every crash window and downstream response
The change is safe to release Reviewed PR, CI results and rollout plan Real production behavior after deployment

No tests have been executed for this illustrative case in this manuscript. Any future RSpec snippet should be run in a reproducible fixture and accompanied by the actual versions, commands and results.

Try this: Specify a test that starts two workers with the same event key. What should be asserted about database records and actual business effects? Which assertion would fail if the implementation used check-then-create without atomic protection?

Checkpoint: Identify one verified observation, one claim it supports and one risk that still requires investigation.

5. Evolving Existing Software Through Integrated Workflows

What changes when AI joins the engineering workflow?

Nothing about the Rails product itself needs to become “an AI application” for its engineering workflow to incorporate useful AI capabilities. The consequential change is the engineer’s role in directing the workflow: from mainly implementing a requested change by hand toward shaping the intent, orchestrating authorized capabilities, testing their results, and integrating what has been learned. The engineer may still write the critical code or reject automation altogether.

A practical environment might combine IDE or ChatGPT-based inquiry, GitHub repository and PR workflows, project instructions and Skills for conventions, MCP-connected tools for scoped system access, Hooks where supported for checks, SDKs for specialized orchestration, and CI/CD for reproducible verification. These elements are not inherently trusted or universally compatible. Permissions and evidence are separate from tool connectivity; each configuration must be reviewed in its real environment.

For the hypothetical payment-retry problem, a disciplined flow could connect:

  1. Intent: report the duplicate-effect risk and acceptance criteria.
  2. Inquiry: inspect repository state and relevant evidence with read-only tools.
  3. Plan: propose one bounded design change, negative tests and failure handling.
  4. Implementation: create a reviewable diff under approved permissions.
  5. Verification: run appropriate tests, review CI findings and record unknowns.
  6. Human decision: approve or reject the PR and a controlled release.
  7. Feedback: observe retry rates and unexpected effects, then revise the understanding.

This sequence is a proposed workflow, not a report of a completed deployment. The actions may form loops; a failed test or unexpected production observation should return the investigation to an earlier decision. NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework offers relevant Govern, Map, Measure and Manage perspectives, but it does not mandate the workflow above.

Proposed interaction sequence — not an executed deployment

The sequence shows intended authority and evidence handoffs. It does not assert that any agent, CI job, or release ran for the hypothetical payment example.

An agent could prepare the investigation and propose tests; CI could execute predetermined checks; the engineer still owns the decision about coverage, business impact and release authority. Integrating tools does not eliminate system boundaries or responsibility.

Try this: Sketch the developer–agent–repository–CI–reviewer sequence. Mark where read-only access becomes write access, where evidence is produced, and where a human must approve a consequential change.

Checkpoint: Which parts of this workflow are automated actions, and which are engineering judgments that cannot be inferred from an agent’s self-report?

6. AI-Native Products Versus AI-Native Engineering

Are we building an AI-Native product, or practicing AI-Native engineering?

It helps to ask two independent questions:

Question Example
**What are we building?** An application where model-backed reasoning is a core product capability
**How are we building and evolving it?** A conventional Rails service maintained through integrated, reviewable AI-assisted workflows

Two-axis thought experiment

  Conventional engineering workflow AI-integrated engineering workflow
**Non-AI product** Rails service developed conventionally Rails service evolved with bounded agents, tests and review
**Model-powered product** LLM feature built with ordinary development processes LLM feature built with integrated and governed agentic workflows

This matrix is an editorial distinction, not a maturity ranking or a standardized taxonomy.

These dimensions can intersect, but neither implies the other. A product may rely on an LLM while its development process remains conventional. A deterministic application may be built through agent-supported workflows without adopting any model in production.

AI-Native Engineering is our working editorial framing for a process that connects human intent, system context, bounded agentic work, verification, operational feedback and revisable understanding throughout software’s evolution. Public usage varies; it is not a single industry-wide standard or a badge awarded once an agent can run commands.

Nor does every problem benefit from an LLM. An explicit idempotency invariant is generally a deterministic engineering problem. Contrast it with ambiguous natural-language support-ticket classification: a probabilistic model might be useful there, but only after comparison with simpler baselines, error evaluation, human escalation and an operating plan. This second case is a thought experiment, not a measured result.

Try this: Classify these two axes for your team’s most recent feature. Which parts need intelligence, and which need straightforward, testable behavior?

Checkpoint: Can you explain why AI-enabled development does not automatically turn the resulting software into an AI-Native product?

Transfer — What would you do differently on Monday?

Choose one existing repository and a low-risk change. Write down its Use Case, desired outcome, known constraints, unknowns and source-of-truth files. Delegate only read-only inquiry first. Request a proposed diff and targeted tests. Record the evidence, note what remains unverified, and keep normal human review and deployment permissions.

Do this for a traditional software feature before choosing more complex multi-agent arrangements. The goal is not to install the largest toolkit: it is to make one engineering decision more informed and one change more verifiable.

Conclusion — Understanding in action

AI-Native Engineering, as framed here, is a change in the operating model of engineering, not merely a faster code-generation technique or a property of an AI-powered product. Intent defines what matters; inquiry and context establish what is understood and unknown; appropriately bounded tools and agents help carry out work; tests, reviews, and operational observations provide evidence; and the resulting understanding remains revisable.

The engineer increasingly acts as an orchestrator of engineering processes—connecting IDEs, ChatGPT, GitHub, Skills, Hooks, MCP, SDKs, and CI/CD where suitable—without surrendering direct coding skills, release authority, or accountability. Success means more than an agent completing a task: it means knowing why the change is warranted, what the evidence actually supports, what remains uncertain, and who is responsible for the next decision.

The approach applies both to new model-powered products and to established deterministic software, including systems already in production. The essential movement is from isolated prompts and implementations toward continuously informed, governed, and verifiable software evolution.

Next practical article (proposed): Building an AI-Native Engineering Environment with GitHub Copilot — From an Existing Rails Repository to Integrated Agentic Workflows. That practical tutorial can cover IDE setup, Instructions, Skills, MCP, permissions, PR/CI and release gates with executable examples. This article intentionally establishes the conceptual model first.

Related reading

For a separate, symbolic exploration of the developer’s changing relationship with AI and evolving understanding, see The Developer’s AI Journey: From Prompts to AI-Native Engineering.

References and status

  • Sidekiq — Best Practices
  • Ruby on Rails — Active Record Transactions
  • METR — Early-2025 AI and experienced open-source developers
  • DORA — 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development
  • Model Context Protocol — specification (2026-07-28)
  • GitHub Docs — Copilot agent mode
  • NIST — AI Risk Management Framework Core

entry.content:
🧠 Insight

The journey is not about mastering AI. It is about transforming understanding.

OPEN MIND · INQUIRY · ENGINEERING · XXI → 0

There has never been so much AI within a developer's reach—and perhaps never so much uncertainty about where to begin.

One day we are discovering autocomplete. Soon we are debating prompts, vibe coding, context windows, agentic workflows, MCP, Skills, AI-driven delivery, and AI-native systems. Every week offers another tool, another framework, another claim that everything has changed.

What does a developer actually need to learn? And more importantly, what is changing in the way we understand and build software?

Contents

  • Act II — The Turning Point
  • Act III — Integration and Return
  • The 22 Major Arcana as three interwoven paths

A map, not a maturity ladder

The Fool’s Journey, a popular narrative interpretation of the 22 Major Arcana, gives us an intriguing metaphor. The Fool (0) represents openness: the willingness to step forward without possessing every answer. The World (XXI) represents integration: seeing connections that were invisible at the beginning. But the story does not end there. XXI returns to 0. Experience changes the traveler; uncertainty remains.

This is a literary and educational metaphor, not a claim that tarot predicts technological progress. Nor is it a prescription that every developer must encounter every tool in the same order. Different capabilities overlap; they are not badges on a universal career ladder.

The central question

Instead of asking “Which tool comes after prompts?”, ask “What problem am I trying to understand, and what capability would help me investigate it responsibly?”

Major Arcana imagery: Rider–Waite–Smith (Pam-A) collection, illustrated by Pamela Colman Smith (1909–1910), via Wikimedia Commons. Original artwork is public domain; card images load from Wikimedia Commons and require an internet connection unless downloaded locally.

Three paths through the journey

The Secret of the Sphinx explores a symbolic reading of three paths: Osiris, Thoth–Sopdet, and Horus. We can borrow that interpretive lens for software engineering without suggesting that it is an established historical taxonomy of tarot or a mandated order of technological progress.

These are three interwoven paths with specific Arcana sequences, not three compulsory levels. Transformation challenges assumptions; awakening deepens observation and understanding; experience tests understanding through action. Their symbolic lessons can overlap in practice, but the card sequences shown below retain their defined order.

PATH I

Osiris · Transformation

What must I reconsider or leave behind?

From the assumption that productivity means typing code, to questioning premature trust, obsolete habits, and fragile automation.

Developer practice: review assumptions, recognize failure modes, and redesign the process.

PATH II

Thoth–Sopdet · Awakening

What am I beginning to understand?

Prompts, context, tools, MCP, agents, and Skills expand what can be explored—but do not automatically establish what is true.

Developer practice: investigate, ask better questions, and make uncertainty explicit.

PATH III

Horus · Experience

How can I apply and validate what I understand?

Turn hypotheses into bounded workflows, useful software, tests, reviews, evaluations, and accountable AI-native design.

Developer practice: build, measure, verify, and learn from consequences.

0 · Open mind→ Transformation · Awakening · Experience→ XXI · Integration↻ 0 · Renewed inquiry

Three paths, one evolving understanding. Transformation changes our assumptions. Awakening changes what we notice. Experience tests what we build. None of them removes the need for the others.

The arcana remain the symbolic encounters of the story; these paths describe different ways to interpret what happens during those encounters. For example, the Hanged Man (XII) belongs to the Path of Horus, the Tower (XVI) to the Path of Osiris, and Justice (XI) to the Path of Thoth–Sopdet. These correspondences are editorial interpretations rather than fixed tarot rules.

Act I — The Awakening

Explore Arcana 0–IVOpen mind, code completion, prompts, creativity and workflows
ARCANUM 0

The Fool — An open mind

Imagine a developer in a familiar environment: editor, terminal, tests, pull requests, deadlines. A new assistant appears in the IDE. Curiosity competes with skepticism: Will this help? Will I lose my skills? Should I trust it?

An open mind is not unconditional enthusiasm. It is the willingness to experiment without surrendering judgment. The first change is not in the stack; it is in the posture toward the unknown.

ARCANUM I

The Magician — Code completion

An intelligently suggested line, a function, a test scaffold: the developer still chooses the direction, while AI reduces friction at the keyboard.

The small convenience raises a much larger question: If AI can complete code, what else could it help me do?

ARCANUM II

The High Priestess — Prompts and context

Conversation expands beyond completion: explain an unfamiliar Rails service, surface trade-offs, compare approaches, or challenge an assumption.

Strong prompting depends on context, constraints, examples, and iterative inquiry—not magical wording or presumed correctness.

ARCANUM III

The Empress — Vibe coding and creation

Natural-language generation accelerates prototypes. An idea becomes an interface or small product quickly enough to discover what the developer actually wants.

But vibe coding, especially without serious code inspection, is not the same as production-grade engineering. Demonstrating possibility is not proving reliability.

ARCANUM IV

The Emperor — Workflows and structure

Instead of collecting disconnected answers, turn work into a reproducible sequence: research, design, implement, test, review, publish. Make inputs, checks, and outputs explicit.

The emphasis shifts from one useful answer to a dependable way of working.

WEAK REQUEST

“Refactor this job.”

ENGINEERING REQUEST

“Identify failure modes in this Sidekiq job, preserve idempotency, propose alternatives, and show which assumptions require tests.”

Act II — The Turning Point

Explore Arcana V–XVISkills, tools, agency, verification, perspective and risks
ARCANUM V

The Hierophant — Skills and tradition

Expertise can be captured in reusable Skills: procedures, project conventions, examples, review criteria, and domain knowledge.

The question changes from What should I prompt? to Which practice can my team repeat and inspect?

ARCANUM VI

The Lovers — Human–AI collaboration

AI can propose and execute. The developer still frames intent, defines boundaries, evaluates trade-offs, and accepts responsibility.

Good collaboration is neither total delegation nor refusal to delegate; it is a deliberate division of work.

ARCANUM VII

The Chariot — Tools and MCP

Tools expose concrete actions; MCP provides a protocol for connecting approved capabilities and context. An assistant can reach repositories, APIs, documentation, and tests.

Access expands what can be done, but permissions and provenance must remain explicit.

Tools / MCPAccess to systems and actions
AgentsPlanning and multistep execution
SkillsReusable ways of doing work
VerificationEvidence that results meet expectations
ARCANUM VIII

Strength — Controlled autonomy

Agents can plan and perform multistep work, including editing files, running checks, and proposing a pull request.

Controlled autonomy requires bounded goals, permissions, traceability, checkpoints, and human approval where warranted.

ARCANUM IX

The Hermit — Reflection and discernment

When a result looks convincing, the developer must still ask: How do I know?

Reflection means examining assumptions, reading the code, reviewing generated explanations, and seeking evidence beyond fluent output.

ARCANUM X

Wheel of Fortune — A changing landscape

Models, products, and workflows evolve. What works today may change with the next release or context window.

Keep the engineering principles portable: explicit requirements, reproducible tests, observability, and the ability to recover safely.

ARCANUM XI

Justice — Verification and accountability

A passing test does not necessarily prove the right behavior was tested. A link does not automatically supply evidence. A successful tool call is not a validated business outcome.

Verification joins correctness, security, provenance, and accountable review. Capability is not correctness.

ARCANUM XII

The Hanged Man — A change in perspective

This is the turning point: producing more code faster is not the same as knowing what should be built, why, and how to determine whether it fulfills the intent.

Code becomes an expression of understanding, never its substitute.

ARCANUM XIII

Death — Letting go of assumptions

Some assumptions must be released: that professional value is measured by lines typed, that every task needs an agent, or that a demo proves readiness.

Leaving those assumptions behind makes more room for domain understanding and sound engineering choices.

ARCANUM XIV

Temperance — Human–AI integration

Balance automation with tests, architecture, observability, human communication, and operational constraints.

The goal is not to choose human or machine, but to design a process in which each contributes what can be justified and verified.

ARCANUM XV

The Devil — The dependency trap

Convenience can become dependence: unfamiliar code is accepted, investigation is skipped, and authority is delegated without safeguards.

The danger is less the presence of AI than the disappearance of independent judgment.

ARCANUM XVI

The Tower — Failure reveals the architecture

Reality intervenes: a payment job retries twice, a data migration violates invariants, or an agent changes the wrong files.

Failure asks a sharper question: What did our process fail to understand?

Capability is not correctness.

AI can generate options. Engineering judgment evaluates constraints, evidence, risks, and consequences.

Act III — Integration and Return

Explore Arcana XVII–XXINew perspectives, uncertainty, clarity and AI-native integration
ARCANUM XVII

The Star — Renewed vision

A renewed engineering vision sees relationships among people, knowledge, tools, models, policies, and evaluations.

We can pursue better outcomes rather than simply more generated output.

ARCANUM XVIII

The Moon — Uncertainty and evidence

Models generate claims; systems retrieve sources; neither operation proves understanding. Uncertainty must be represented rather than concealed.

Distinguish output, source, evidence, claim, and understanding, and keep unresolved questions visible.

ARCANUM XIX

The Sun — Clarity through inquiry

Clarity grows when intent is explicit and observations can be tested against expectations.

The objective is not certainty about everything. It is an honest, revisable account of what the system does and why.

ARCANUM XX

Judgement — Reimagining architecture

The architectural question emerges: when should AI participate in a running product rather than only in the development workflow?

Think about model inference, tools, context, evaluation, governed actions, and feedback as designed capabilities—not magic defaults.

ARCANUM XXI

The World — Integration, not completion

A wider picture comes into view. Prompts, Skills, agents, workflows, and models become design choices in service of people and real constraints.

The World is integration, not final mastery. From XXI the developer returns to 0—with fresh questions and a wider perspective.

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE

AI-Assisted

AI helps developers build.

Example: GitHub Copilot suggests Rails code, explains a service, or drafts a test for human review.

ENGINEERING WORKFLOW

AI-Driven

AI drives bounded parts of the process.

Example: An agent proposes a change, runs tests, and prepares a pull request for human approval.

PRODUCT ARCHITECTURE

AI-Native

AI participates in the running system.

Example: A product integrates model inference, tools, context, evaluation, and governed actions.

These are working distinctions, not an official certification ladder. An AI-native product can still be developed with traditional tooling; an AI-assisted team can ship entirely deterministic software.

The 22 Major Arcana as three interwoven paths

The card associations below are interpretive, not technological milestones. Begin with 0 — The Fool above, then expand any of the three paths to explore its seven-card sequence as illustrated cards with engineering context. The final card, XXI — The World, returns to 0. We use the common Rider–Waite–Smith numbering, where Strength is VIII and Justice is XI.

A practical engineering example

Suppose you are asked to improve the reliability of payment processing in a Rails application.

An autocomplete-only approach helps write another retry method. A prompt-first approach asks for recommendations. A workflow-driven approach inspects the code, develops a failure model, implements changes, runs checks, and requires review. With tools and agents, much of that work can be coordinated across repository, CI, and documentation. With Skills, project-specific conventions can become repeatable.

But none of those capabilities can replace the critical questions: Is the operation idempotent? What happens under duplicate delivery? Which side effects can be reversed? Which invariant proves business correctness? Who approves the change?

OUTPUT-CENTRIC

“The AI wrote a retry policy.”

UNDERSTANDING-CENTRIC

“We identified the failure modes, tested the invariants, and can explain why the recovery policy is appropriate.”

The deepest gain is not the number of generated lines. It is the ability to discover, test, and preserve a more accurate account of the system.

Where are you in the journey?

Do not measure your progress by how many new products you have installed. Ask which questions you can now answer:

  • Exploring? Can you explain what you want AI to help you discover?
  • Prompting? Can you supply context, constraints, and verification criteria?
  • Automating? Can your workflow fail visibly and recover safely?
  • Connecting tools? Can you describe what the system is permitted to access and change?
  • Delegating to agents? Can you tell the difference between execution success and task correctness?
  • Designing AI-native systems? Can you represent uncertainty, audit decisions, and evaluate outcomes?
Compass, not checklist

Find your current question. Choose the smallest capability that helps answer it. Verify what you learned. Repeat.

XXI → 0: the return

The Fool begins without knowing. The World arrives with a wider understanding. But wisdom is not the absence of uncertainty. It is the ability to return to uncertainty with better questions, stronger methods, and greater responsibility.

The engineer who first discovered intelligent autocomplete is not quite the same engineer who now considers agent orchestration, Skills, evidence, or AI-native architecture. Yet the most important capability remains recognizable: an open mind prepared to investigate what is actually happening.

Every new tool expands what a developer can do. Every new understanding transforms what a developer can become.

The World is not the end of the journey. It is the moment the Fool discovers a new beginning.

The Journey as a Semantic Model

The twenty-two Arcana can be described once as a set of contextual meanings, then related through three interwoven paths. In this interpretation, Context situates each card in AI engineering, Light expresses its constructive possibility, Shadow explores its limitations, and Insight captures a question or understanding that may emerge. These are interpretive perspectives, not proven properties of the cards or evidence about AI systems.

The Mermaid diagram presents the overall relationships. Expand the Ruby DSL below to explore the full model of the 22 Arcana, their AI contexts, three paths, and the return XXI → 0. This is an illustrative Ruby DSL, not a working parser or executable implementation.

The journey does not repeat itself. It unfolds again from a different understanding.

Freedom and the movement of inquiry

The developer's journey also invites a question about the person using the tools: what shapes the way we look, decide, and act? A new capability can change our work while leaving our dependence on authority, approval, or familiar explanations unexamined.

Krishnamurti places freedom from conditioning at the heart of inquiry. Yet freedom is not merely a reward at the end of a prescribed path: he connects it with observation in daily life, including the images, motives, and divisions that shape perception. His Core of the Teachings questions both psychological techniques and the separation between observer and observed.

The negative approach here means examining what obstructs perception, rather than prescribing an ideal image of a liberated person. Even the wish to become free can carry fear, reward, or a projected identity. Negation does not mean suppressing feelings or rejecting practical knowledge; his Amsterdam talk of 14 May 1969 distinguishes the need for technical knowledge from observing oneself through accumulated psychological conclusions.

Interpretive scope. These associations are our symbolic reading inspired by Krishnamurti. He did not teach a Tarot system or a 22-stage method. The cards name persistent perspectives; attention can question any of them, including this map.

One vocabulary, another inquiry

The Ruby DSL below retains the article's journey, arcana, context, light, shadow, and insight vocabulary. Here, light names a possibility to examine, shadow a possible interference, and insight an editorial proposition. These fields neither rank people nor certify an experience of insight.

The same three paths reference the same ordered cards as the earlier model. Their sequences support a symbolic reading; the inquiry itself may branch, return, or pause. For example, observing an attachment at XV may reopen the motive at I, while a question about authority at V may change how we approach a relationship at VI.

XXI returns to 0. We call that renewal event: 22: an event, not a twenty-third card. The record remains available, but its conclusions need not determine every new encounter. This example uses cycle for the return declaration because return is a Ruby keyword.
